- Wikipedia: Information about: Nebulin
Section: Introduction
Nebulin[5] is an actin-binding protein which is localized to the thin filament of the sarcomeres in skeletal muscle. Nebulin in humans is coded for by the gene NEB. It is a very large protein (600–900 kDa) and binds as many as 200 actin monomers. Because its length is proportional to thin filament length, it is believed that nebulin acts as a thin filament "ruler" and regulates thin filament length during sarcomere assembly.[6]  Other functions of nebulin, such as a role in cell signaling, remain uncertain. Nebulin has also been shown to regulate actin-myosin interactions by inhibiting ATPase activity in a calcium-calmodulin sensitive manner.[7] Nebulin has also been shown to regulate actin-myosin interactions by inhibiting ATPase activity in a calcium-calmodulin sensitive manner.[7] Mutations in nebulin cause some cases of the autosomal recessive disorder nemaline myopathy.[8] A smaller member of the nebulin protein family, termed nebulette, is expressed in cardiac muscle. A smaller member of the nebulin protein family, termed nebulette, is expressed in cardiac muscle.
Section: Structure
The structure of the SH3 domain of nebulin was determined by protein nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy.[9] The SH3 domain from nebulin is composed of 60 amino acid residues, of which 30 percent is in the beta sheet secondary structure (7 strands; 18 residues).
Section: Knockout phenotype
As of 2007, two knockout mouse models for nebulin have been developed to better understand its in vivo function.  Bang and colleagues[10] demonstrated that nebulin-knockout mice die postnatally, have reduced thin filament length, and impaired contractile function.  Postnatal sarcomere disorganization and degeneration occurred rapidly in these mice, indicating the nebulin is essential for maintaining the structural integrity of myofibrils.  Witt and colleagues[11] had similar results in their mice, which also died postnatally with reduced thin filament length and contractile function.  These nebulin-knockout mice are being investigated as animal models of nemaline myopathy.
-------------------Information about: Tropomyosin
Section: Tropomyosin and the actin skeleton
Tropomyosins are often categorised into two groups: muscle tropomyosin isoforms and nonmuscle tropomyosin isoforms. Muscle tropomyosin isoforms are involved in regulating interactions between actin and myosin in the muscle sarcomere and play a pivotal role in regulated muscle contraction. Nonmuscle tropomyosin isoforms function in both muscle and nonmuscle cells, and are involved in a range of cellular pathways that control and regulate the cell's cytoskeleton and other key cellular functions. The actin filament system that is involved in regulating these cellular pathways is more complex than the actin filament systems that regulates muscle contraction. The contractile system relies upon 4 actin filament isoforms and 5 tropomyosin isoforms,[1] whereas the actin filament system of the cytoskeleton uses two actin filament isoforms and over 40 tropomyosin isoforms.[1][2]
Section: Specific roles and functions
Skeletal muscle is composed of large, multi-nucleated cells (muscle fibers). Each muscle fiber is packed with longitudinal arrays of myofibrils. Myofibrils are composed of repeating protein structures or sarcomeres, the basic functional unit of skeletal muscle. The sarcomere is a highly structured protein array, consisting of interdigitating thick and thin filaments, where the thin filaments are tethered to a protein structure, the Z-line. The dynamic interaction between the thick and thin filaments results in muscle contraction. Myosin belongs to a family of motor proteins, and the muscle isoforms of this family comprise the thick filament. The thin filament is made of the skeletal muscle isoforms of actin. Each myosin protein 'paddles' along the thin actin filament, repeatedly binding to myosin-binding sites along the actin filament, ratcheting and letting go. In effect, the thick filament moves or slides along the thin filament, resulting in muscle contraction. This process is known as the sliding filament model. The binding of the myosin heads to the muscle actin is a highly regulated process. The thin filament is made of actin, tropomyosin, and troponin. The contraction of skeletal muscle is triggered by nerve impulses that in turn stimulate the release of Ca2+. The release of Ca2+ from the sarcoplasmic reticulum causes an increase in the concentration of Ca2+ in the cytosol. Calcium ions then bind to troponin, which is associated with tropomyosin. Binding causes changes in the shape of troponin and subsequently causes the tropomyosin isoform to shift its position on the actin filament. This shifting in position exposes the myosin-binding sites on the actin filament, allowing the myosin heads of the thick filament to bind to the thin filament.
-------------------Information about: Nebulina
Section: Estructura
Actina (Superfície Àcida): L'actina és una proteïna globular amb un punt isoelèctric (pI) àcid, al voltant de 5.2.[17] Al pH fisiològic (~ 7.4), que és molt superior al seu pI, l’actina tindrà una càrrega neta negativa. Això és coherent amb el fet que molts dels seus residus, com l’àcid aspàrtic (Asp) i l’àcid glutàmic (Glu), estan desprotonats a aquest pH i, per tant, porten grups carboxilat (COO⁻). Els pKa mitjans mesurats per residus d’Asp i Glu són al voltant de ~3.5 i ~4.2, respectivament.[18] Nebulina (Motius Bàsics): En el motiu d'unió SDXXYK, la lisina (K) juga un paper clau en l’ancoratge a l’actina.[19] El grup amino de la cadena lateral de la lisina té un pKa d’aproximadament 10.5.[20] A pH 7.4 (molt per sota del seu pKa), el grup amino de la lisina estarà protonat (NH₃⁺) i, per tant, portarà una càrrega neta positiva. Aquesta càrrega positiva afavoreix l’atracció cap a regions carregades negativament de l’actina. Dins del motiu SDXXYK, els diferents residus contribueixen al posicionament i estabilització de l'enllaç, i la lisina (pel seu important paper funcional i la seva càrrega positiva) és la que estableix interaccions directes amb l'actina.[21] NRAP (Nebulin-related anchoring protein): s'organitza en dominis repetitius i intervé en l'assemblatge de les miofibril·les [11] Nebulette: és més curta i predominant a la regió del disc Z del múscul cardíac, on contribueix a la formació de miofilaments. Té una organització en dominis semblant a la nebulina, amb els motius SDXXYK i WLKGIGW.[14] LASP-1 i LASP-2 (LIM and SH3 protein): és una proteïna més petita amb dominis LIM i SH3 implicada en l'organització del citoesquelet.[11]
Section: Patologies associades
Miopatia nemalínica (NM): és una de les formes més freqüents de miopatia no distròfica, sense reemplaçament muscular massiu ni progressió degenerativa, i es caracteritza per la presència de cossos nemalínics. Està associada a variants patogèniques del gen NEB. [38] Aquestes mutacions típicament recessives, redueixen significativament els nivells de nebulina en el múscul esquelètic, fet que provoca filaments prims d’actina més curts i no uniformes.[39] També s'ha observat una alteració de l'estat “super‑relaxed state” de la miosina, que incrementa el consum energètic en fibres musculars en repòs a causa dels canvis en proteïnes implicades en el metabolisme muscular.[40] Com a conseqüència, els pacients presenten debilitat muscular generalitzada, hipotonia, dificultat per caminar i, en formes greus, complicacions respiratòries.[41][42] Miopatia distal: es presenten grans delecions en el gen NEB (entre 52‑97 exons) associades a debilitat predominant dels dorsiflexors, extensors de dits i flexors del coll. La progressió és habitualment més lenta que en altres miopaties.[43] Un estudi realitzat en 35 famílies va mostrar que aquestes delecions poden heretar-se de manera dominant i causar miopatia distal predominant, fet que amplia el ventall fenotípic de la nebulina.[44] Miopatia core-rod: es caracteritza per la presència simultània de cores (zones desorganitzades de la fibra amb pèrdua de funcionalitat) i de rods (agregats nemalínics d’actina i proteïnes sarcomèriques). Aquesta malaltia recessiva es deu a mutacions truncants del gen NEB que interrompen la síntesi de la proteïna i provoquen debilitat muscular generalitzada de llarga evolució.[45] Miopatia perinatal letal: determinades mutacions severes poden originar formes perinatals letals de miopatia, que inclouen aquinèsia fetal (absència de moviment), síndrome de pterígies múltiples (contractures congènites) i hipoplàsia pulmonar.[46]
Section: Bibliografia
Journal of Molecular Biology, 402, 1, 9-2010, pàg. 38–51. DOI: 10.1016/j.jmb.2010.07.011. PMID: 20643138.

full_data.long_answer: The gene responsible for approximately half of all recorded cases of nemaline myopathy is NEB, which encodes the protein nebulin. Nebulin is an actin-binding protein that is localized to the thin filament of sarcomeres in skeletal muscle. Its structure allows it to act as a 'thin filament ruler,' as its length is proportional to the thin filament length, thereby regulating filament assembly and stability. Mutations in the NEB gene result in a reduction or functional impairment of nebulin, which in turn causes abnormalities in the structure of the thin filament. This disruption of thin filament architecture is a major contributor to the development of nemaline myopathy, a congenital neuromuscular disorder characterized by muscle weakness and the presence of rod-like structures (nemaline bodies) in muscle fibers.

Section: Introduction
Nebulin[5] is an actin-binding protein which is localized to the thin filament of the sarcomeres in skeletal muscle. Nebulin in humans is coded for by the gene NEB. It is a very large protein (600–900 kDa) and binds as many as 200 actin monomers. Section: Structure
The structure of the SH3 domain of nebulin was determined by protein nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy.[9] The SH3 domain from nebulin is composed of 60 amino acid residues, of which 30 percent is in the beta sheet secondary structure (7 strands; 18 residues).
Section: Knockout phenotype
As of 2007, two knockout mouse models for nebulin have been developed to better understand its in vivo function.  Bang and colleagues[10] demonstrated that nebulin-knockout mice die postnatally, have reduced thin filament length, and impaired contractile function.  Postnatal sarcomere disorganization and degeneration occurred rapidly in these mice, indicating the nebulin is essential for maintaining the structural integrity of myofibrils.  Witt and colleagues[11] had similar results in their mice, which also died postnatally with reduced thin filament length and contractile function.  These nebulin-knockout mice are being investigated as animal models of nemaline myopathy.

Section: Tropomyosin and the actin skeleton
Tropomyosins are often categorised into two groups: muscle tropomyosin isoforms and nonmuscle tropomyosin isoforms. Muscle tropomyosin isoforms are involved in regulating interactions between actin and myosin in the muscle sarcomere and play a pivotal role in regulated muscle contraction. Nonmuscle tropomyosin isoforms function in both muscle and nonmuscle cells, and are involved in a range of cellular pathways that control and regulate the cell's cytoskeleton and other key cellular functions. The actin filament system that is involved in regulating these cellular pathways is more complex than the actin filament systems that regulates muscle contraction. The contractile system relies upon 4 actin filament isoforms and 5 tropomyosin isoforms,[1] whereas the actin filament system of the cytoskeleton uses two actin filament isoforms and over 40 tropomyosin isoforms.[1][2]

Each myosin protein 'paddles' along the thin actin filament, repeatedly binding to myosin-binding sites along the actin filament, ratcheting and letting go. In effect, the thick filament moves or slides along the thin filament, resulting in muscle contraction. This process is known as the sliding filament model. The release of Ca2+ from the sarcoplasmic reticulum causes an increase in the concentration of Ca2+ in the cytosol. Calcium ions then bind to troponin, which is associated with tropomyosin. Binding causes changes in the shape of troponin and subsequently causes the tropomyosin isoform to shift its position on the actin filament. This shifting in position exposes the myosin-binding sites on the actin filament, allowing the myosin heads of the thick filament to bind to the thin filament.
